title: 〜たところ (result)
meaning: You did something, and as a result you found out a fact or got a certain outcome. Like “I tried ..., and it turned out ...”.
connection: Verb た-form + ところ、+ result (usually something that already happened)

senses.label: Did it and found out
senses.meaning: The first part is an action the speaker did on purpose. The second part is the result or fact learned afterwards, often something new or surprising. The second part is in the past tense.
senses.connection: Volitional verb た-form + ところ、…た (common: 「調べたところ」, 「聞いてみたところ」, 「問い合わせたところ」)
examples: I asked a station attendant, and apparently the train is running 30 minutes late.
I looked it up online and found that the shop had already closed down.
I had a doctor examine me, and was told it was just a cold.

senses.label: Expected or unexpected result
senses.meaning: The result can be what you hoped for, or the opposite of what you expected. For an unexpected result you often see 「〜たところ、意外にも」. In written style you also see 「〜たところが」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ところ、(意外にも / 思ったより) …た
examples: I consulted my teacher, and they gladly agreed to help.
I tried a new method, and it went better than I expected.

notes: The second part must be a fact that happened or became known after the first action. It can't be the speaker's intention, an order, or a request. ✕「調べたところ、行きましょう」.
The first part is usually a deliberate action, often with 「〜てみた」: 「やってみたところ」.
Without 「、」, 「〜たところだ」 means “have just done”. That is a different usage.
「〜たところで」 means “even if ... (it's no use)”. Completely different meaning.

daily.title: Reporting what you found out
daily.description: Telling your family what you learned on the phone.
daily.example: I called the restaurant, and they were fully booked today.

daily.title: Trying something new
daily.description: Sharing your impression with a friend after trying a product.
daily.example: I tried this toner, and my skin got better.

daily.title: Reading a news report
daily.description: News often uses it to present the results of an investigation.
daily.example: When residents were asked, it turned out that many people feel anxious.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Politely reporting the result after checking something.
work.example: I checked with the client, and they said the delivery date is next Friday.

work.title: Writing a survey report
work.description: Explaining the results of an experiment or survey in a report or paper.
work.example: When a questionnaire was conducted, about 70% answered that they were satisfied.

etymology: 「ところ」 is written 「所」 and originally means “place”. It extended to mean “moment, stage”. 「〜たところ」 first meant “at the moment I had done ...”, and then “after doing ... (I found)”, introducing a result.

similar.title: 〜たところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜たところだ」 ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means “have just done”. This pattern is followed by 「、」 and a result clause: “I did ..., and found ...”.

similar.title: 〜たら〜た (discovery)
similar.explanation: Both can mean “when I did ..., I found ...”. 「〜たら」 is more conversational and often describes something you happened to notice. 「〜たところ」 is a bit formal and is used for the result of a purposeful check or inquiry.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: 「〜たところで」 means “even if ... (it won't help)”, and the second part is usually negative, as in 「今から行ったところで間に合わない」. Similar form, very different meaning.

similar.title: 〜結果
similar.explanation: 「〜た結果」 stresses the final outcome of effort or a process, and is more formal. 「〜たところ」 simply tells what you found out after doing something; it doesn't have to be the fruit of effort.

meaning: Something else happens just when you are at a certain moment or in a certain situation. Often someone arrives or a call comes in, interrupting or affecting what is going on.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / た-form + ところに・ところへ; い-adjective + ところに

senses.label: Just when ..., someone came
senses.meaning: The first part is the situation the speaker is in; the second part is something that suddenly happens at that moment. The second part usually has a verb of movement or appearance, such as 「来る」, 「現れる」 or 「電話がかかる」. 「ところへ」 stresses the sense of “arriving” a bit more than 「ところに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form (about to) / ている-form (in the middle of) / た-form (just finished) + ところに・ところへ + 来る / かかってくる etc.
examples: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came to visit.
A phone call came while I was taking a bath.
Just as we finished talking, the department manager walked in.

senses.label: Perfect timing
senses.meaning: 「いいところに」 and 「ちょうどいいところへ」 mean someone came at just the right time. Very common in conversation. It can also show that a situation gets worse: 「困っているところに、さらに〜」.
senses.connection: いい / ちょうどいい + ところに・ところへ + 来た; verb ている-form + ところに + さらに…
examples: Oh, you came at just the right time. Give me a hand.
While I was lost and didn't know what to do, a kind person spoke to me.

notes: The second part is “something that happens”, so it is usually not the speaker's own deliberate action.
If a noun or な-adjective comes before 「ところ」 (「静かなところに」), it usually means “place”. That is not this pattern.
「ところに」 and 「ところへ」 mean almost the same. With a movement verb both work; 「ところへ」 feels more dynamic.

daily.title: A friend shows up at the right time
daily.description: A friend appears just when you need help.
daily.example: You came at just the right time. Help me carry this box.

daily.title: Interrupted during a meal
daily.description: Complaining to your family about a sales call during dinner.
daily.example: A sales call came in while I was eating.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Novels often use it to bring a new character on stage.
daily.example: While the two were talking, a strange man appeared.

work.title: Someone enters a meeting
work.description: Describing to a colleague what happened at a meeting.
work.example: Just as we were about to start the meeting, the president arrived.

work.title: More work when you're busy
work.description: Complaining to a colleague about work piling up.
work.example: I'm busy with a deadline, and on top of that I was given a new task.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place”, and was extended to a point in time, “moment, scene”. Adding 「に」 or 「へ」, which mark direction or destination, gives “(something) came to this moment”, that is, “just when ..., ... happened”.

similar.title: 〜ところを
similar.explanation: 「〜ところを」 is usually followed by verbs that act directly on that scene, such as 「見る」, 「見つかる」 or 「助ける」, often in the passive. 「〜ところに／へ」 is followed by something appearing or arriving, such as 「来る」 or 「電話がかかる」.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「〜最中に」 stresses being interrupted right in the middle of something, usually after 「ている」 or noun + の. 「〜ところに」 can also be used for “about to” or “just finished”.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜ところだ」 only describes what stage an action is at. 「〜ところに／へ」 adds “something that happened” at that stage.

meaning: While someone is in a certain scene or situation, another person does something to it (sees it, interrupts it, helps, etc.). Also used in polite set phrases like “when you are so busy”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / た-form, い-adjective, noun + の + ところを

senses.label: Caught while ...
senses.meaning: The first part is the scene someone is in; the second part is what another person does to that scene. Common verbs are 「見る」, 「見つかる」, 「呼び止める」 and 「起こす」, often in the passive. Usually unwelcome for the person.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / dictionary form + ところを + 見られる / 見つかる / 捕まる etc.
examples: My teacher saw me sleeping in class.
I was stopped by a reporter just as I was leaving home.
The thief was caught by the police as he was running out of the shop.

senses.label: Rescued from trouble
senses.meaning: The second part can also be something good, such as 「助ける」 or 「救う」: being helped in a difficult or dangerous situation. It often carries gratitude.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + ところを + 助ける / 救う; 危ない + ところを
examples: While I was lost, a kind person helped me.
Thank you very much for saving me when I was in danger.

senses.label: Polite: when you are ...
senses.meaning: Phrases like 「お忙しいところを」 and 「お休みのところを」 are used to apologize or thank someone: “(sorry to bother you / thank you) when you are so busy / resting”. Common in business and formal settings. 「を」 is sometimes dropped.
senses.connection: お忙しい / お疲れの / お休みの / ご多忙の + ところ(を) + すみません / ありがとうございます
examples: Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a moment?
I'm very sorry to disturb you while you're resting.
Thank you very much for coming today despite the bad weather.

notes: The second part is an action aimed directly at “that scene”, so you often see transitive verbs like 「見る」, 「見つかる」 or 「邪魔する」, or their passive forms.
「〜ところを見ると」 means “judging from ...”. It is a different pattern.
In the polite phrases, 「を」 can be dropped: 「お忙しいところ、ありがとうございます」.

daily.title: Caught being naughty
daily.description: A child tells a friend about getting caught sneaking snacks.
daily.example: My mom caught me eating snacks.

daily.title: Thanking a stranger
daily.description: Thanking someone who helped you when you were in trouble.
daily.example: Thank you for helping me when I was stuck. It really helped.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports describe the scene of an arrest.
daily.example: The man was arrested in the act of trying to steal cash.

work.title: Greeting a client
work.description: Apologizing first when calling or visiting.
work.example: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but could you please check this?

work.title: Opening a speech
work.description: Thanking guests at an event for coming despite their busy schedules.
work.example: Thank you all very much for gathering here today despite your busy schedules.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place”, extended to “scene, moment”. 「を」 marks that scene as the object of the following verb, so what is seen, caught or helped is “that scene of someone doing ...”.

similar.title: 〜ところに・〜ところへ
similar.explanation: 「〜ところに／へ」 is followed by something arriving or happening (someone comes, a call comes in). 「〜ところを」 is followed by an action aimed directly at the scene (see, catch, help).

similar.title: 〜ところを見ると
similar.explanation: 「〜ところを見ると」 means “judging from ...”, and the second part is the speaker's guess, as in 「笑っているところを見ると、合格したらしい」.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「〜最中に」 only says “right in the middle of”, and anything can happen in the second part. With 「〜ところを」, the second part must be an action aimed at that scene.

meaning: Something (usually bad) almost happened, but it actually didn't. Like “nearly ...” or “almost ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった (often with 「もう少しで」, 「危うく」 or 「〜なかったら」)

senses.label: Nearly ...
senses.meaning: Something was about to happen but was avoided in the end. Usually something unwanted, with a sense of relief: “that was close”. Often used with 「もう少しで」, 「危うく」 or 「あやうく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった / ところでした
examples: I almost missed the train.
I nearly got hit by a car.
I overslept and was nearly late for an important exam.

senses.label: If not for ..., would have ...
senses.meaning: Used with conditions like 「〜なかったら」 or 「〜なければ」: “if it hadn't been for ..., ... would have happened”. Used to thank someone or to feel relieved about something.
senses.connection: 〜なかったら / 〜なければ + verb dictionary form + ところだった
examples: If you hadn't told me, things would have gotten really bad.
Without a map, I would have gotten lost.

senses.label: Was just about to ...
senses.meaning: No “nearly” meaning here. It is simply the past of 「〜ところだ」 (about to): at a past moment you were just about to do something. Context tells the two apart.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった (often with 「ちょうど」)
examples: I was just about to call you.

notes: It didn't actually happen, so you can't use 「〜た」. “I almost fell” is 「転ぶところだった」, not 「転んだ」.
「ているところだった」 and 「たところだった」 are past forms of 「〜ところだ」, meaning “was in the middle of ...” and “had just ...”. They don't mean “nearly”.
In casual speech you often hear 「〜ところだったよ」 or 「〜とこだった」.

daily.title: Telling about a close call
daily.description: Telling a friend about something that almost went wrong.
daily.example: I slipped on the stairs and almost fell down.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: A friend's reminder saved you.
daily.example: Good thing you told me. I almost forgot.

daily.title: Relief while shopping
daily.description: Said when you almost bought the wrong thing.
daily.example: If I hadn't checked the size, I would have bought the wrong one.

work.title: Reporting a mistake you avoided
work.description: Explaining to your boss that you almost made an error but caught it in time.
work.example: When I checked, I realized I had almost sent the wrong documents.

work.title: Thanking a coworker
work.description: A coworker helped you meet a deadline.
work.example: Thanks to Tanaka-san, I was saved. I nearly missed the deadline.

etymology: It comes from 「〜ところだ」 (about to) plus the past 「だった」: “I was at the stage of about to ... (but it didn't happen)”. From this came the meaning “nearly ...”.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜ところだ」 describes the stage of an action. 「〜ところだった」 is a derived use specifically for “almost happened, but didn't”.

similar.title: 〜そうになる
similar.explanation: 「〜そうになった」 also means “almost ...”, focusing on signs at that moment, as in 「泣きそうになった」. 「〜ところだった」 stresses “it was one step away from becoming a fact”, and often goes with 「もう少しで」.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: 「〜ばよかった」 is regret about something that did happen. 「〜ところだった」 is relief about something that didn't.

meaning: A situation keeps changing in one direction with no sign of stopping. Like “more and more ...” or “keeps ...ing”.
connection: Dictionary form of a verb of change + 一方だ

senses.label: More and more ...
senses.meaning: Things keep moving in only one direction. Often used for bad changes such as increasing, decreasing or getting worse. It follows verbs of change like 「増える」, 「減る」, 「なる」 or 「上がる」.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + 一方だ (common: 「増える一方だ」, 「悪くなる一方だ」, 「〜ていく一方だ」)
examples: Prices just keep going up.
Lately my work keeps increasing, so I don't even have time to rest.
This town's population keeps shrinking.

senses.label: Past and modifying forms
senses.meaning: It can also be used in the past, 「一方だった」, or before a noun as 「〜一方の」. The meaning stays the same: a steady one-way change.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + 一方だった / 一方である
examples: My father's condition kept getting worse.
Relations between the two countries are steadily deteriorating.

notes: It must follow a verb that expresses change. ✕「勉強する一方だ」.
Mostly used for negative changes, but also for neutral ones.
Don't confuse it with 「〜一方（で）」: 「一方で」 is followed by another clause and shows contrast or parallel actions.

daily.title: Complaining about prices
daily.description: Chatting with family about living costs.
daily.example: Vegetable prices just keep going up, don't they?

daily.title: Talking about weight
daily.description: Telling a friend about your recent weight change.
daily.example: I don't exercise, so my weight just keeps going up.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News often uses it for social problems that keep getting worse.
daily.example: The number of empty houses keeps rising across the country.

work.title: Sales report
work.description: Explaining in a meeting that sales keep falling.
work.example: For the past six months, sales have kept falling.

work.title: Explaining a staff shortage
work.description: Telling your boss about workload and staffing.
work.example: The workload keeps growing, but our staff numbers are going down.

etymology: 「一方」 originally means “one direction, one side”. 「〜一方だ」 is “(changing) in only one direction”, so it expresses change that keeps going one way.

similar.title: 〜ばかりだ (keeps getting ...)
similar.explanation: Both express one-way change. 「〜ばかりだ」 is used almost only for bad changes and carries the speaker's frustration or worry. 「〜一方だ」 is more objective and also works for neutral changes.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: 「〜につれて」 means “as A changes, B also changes”, linking two things. 「〜一方だ」 talks about only one thing changing in one direction.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: 「〜一方で」 is followed by another clause and shows contrast or doing two things at once. 「〜一方だ」 ends the sentence and shows continuing change.

meaning: The same subject has two sides or does two things in parallel, or two different situations are contrasted. Like “on one hand ..., on the other hand ...” or “while ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form (な-adjective + な / である; noun + である) + 一方(で); at the start of a sentence: 「一方」, 「その一方で」

senses.label: Doing two things
senses.meaning: The same person or thing does two things or has two sides at the same time. The two parts are simply listed, with no strong opposition. Like “while also ...” or “besides ...ing”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 一方(で)
examples: He works at a company while also attending university at night.
My mother handles the housework and also volunteers in the community.

senses.label: Contrasting two sides
senses.meaning: Contrasts two opposite sides of the same thing, or two different situations. Like “on the other hand” or “whereas”. Often used for pros and cons.
senses.connection: Plain form (な-adjective + な / である; noun + である) + 一方(で)
examples: This job pays well, but on the other hand there are few days off.
The city is convenient, but the cost of living is high.
While exports are increasing, imports are decreasing.

senses.label: Sentence-initial: on the other hand
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence as 「一方、」 or 「その一方で」, it follows on from the previous sentence and introduces a contrast. Mostly written language and news.
senses.connection: (Previous sentence.) + 一方、/ その一方で、+ next sentence
examples: The population is growing in urban areas. Meanwhile, rural areas are becoming depopulated.
Life has become more convenient. On the other hand, human connections are weakening.

notes: 「で」 can be dropped: 「〜一方、」 is more formal.
After a noun use 「である一方」. ✕「学生の一方で」.
When 「〜一方だ」 ends a sentence, it means “more and more”. That is a different pattern.

daily.title: Talking about a friend's life
daily.description: Describing a friend's many activities.
daily.example: She raises her kids while also working from home.

daily.title: Comparing places to live
daily.description: Discussing the pros and cons of moving with your family.
daily.example: It's close to the station, but the rent is high.

daily.title: Reading news commentary
daily.description: News contrasts two social trends.
daily.example: While online shopping is growing, the number of stores on shopping streets is falling.

work.title: Weighing a proposal
work.description: Objectively comparing a plan's pros and cons in a meeting.
work.example: This plan keeps costs down, but on the other hand it takes time.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Contrasting two sets of data in a report.
work.example: Use among young people increased. Meanwhile, use among older people stayed flat.

etymology: 「一方」 originally means “one direction, one side”. 「〜一方で」 is “on this side ... (on the other side ...)”, which led to the meanings of parallel actions and contrast.

similar.title: 〜反面
similar.explanation: 「〜反面」 only contrasts two opposite sides of the same thing, such as merits and drawbacks. 「〜一方で」 is broader: it can also show doing two things, or contrast two different things.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: 「〜ながら」 means doing two actions at the same moment (studying while listening to music). 「〜一方で」 means doing two things in parallel over a period, not necessarily at the same moment.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「〜に対して」 contrasts the situations of two different subjects (A vs. B) and stresses opposition. 「〜一方で」 can contrast, or simply list.

similar.title: 〜一方だ
similar.explanation: 「〜一方だ」 ends the sentence and means “more and more”. 「〜一方で」 is followed by another clause.

meaning: As the first thing changes, the second changes accordingly. It also means acting according to rules or instructions. Like “as ...” or “in accordance with ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + にしたがって (written: にしたがい)

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: As the first thing changes or develops, the second changes along with it. Both parts are changes.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun expressing change + にしたがって
examples: As you climb the mountain, the temperature drops.
As the times have changed, people's values have changed too.
As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.

senses.label: According to ...
senses.meaning: Acting by following rules, instructions, orders or customs. Like “following ...” or “in accordance with ...”. It often follows nouns like 「指示」, 「規則」, 「矢印」 or 「案内」.
senses.connection: Noun (指示・規則・ルール・案内 etc.) + にしたがって + action
examples: Please evacuate following the staff's instructions.
Please follow the arrows.

notes: In the “as ...” meaning, the second part can't be the speaker's intention or a command. ✕「年をとるにしたがって、運動しよう」.
「にしたがい」 is the written form, common in news and articles.
It can be written with kanji, 「に従って」, but is also often written in kana.

daily.title: Following the GPS
daily.description: A friend says to just follow the car navigation while driving.
daily.example: If you just follow the navigation, you'll be fine.

daily.title: Talking about kids growing up
daily.description: Parents talk about how things change as their child grows.
daily.example: As our child has grown up, we talk less and less.

daily.title: Reading a manual
daily.description: Common in product instructions.
daily.example: Please assemble it following the steps in the manual.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: Telling a new employee about rules to follow.
work.example: Please submit expense claims in accordance with company regulations.

work.title: Analyzing market trends
work.description: Explaining in a report how two trends are linked.
work.example: As the population ages, demand for nursing care services is rising.

etymology: 「したがう」 is written 「従う」 and originally means “to follow, to obey”. 「〜にしたがって」 is “following along with ...”, which gave two meanings: “as (something changes)” and “according to (rules)”.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: In the “as ...” meaning, the two are mostly interchangeable. 「〜につれて」 is more conversational and only shows proportional change, with no “according to” meaning. 「〜にしたがって」 can also mean following rules or instructions.

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: 「〜に伴って」 is more formal and can also mean “happening along with something”, as in 「台風の接近に伴って」. 「〜にしたがって」 focuses on gradual, proportional change.

similar.title: 〜とおりに
similar.explanation: 「〜とおりに」 means “exactly as, the same as ...”. 「〜にしたがって」 means “acting in obedience to (rules, instructions)”, stressing compliance.

meaning: As the first thing changes, the second gradually changes along with it. Like “as ...”.
connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun expressing change + につれて (written: につれ)

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: A change in the first part drives a change in the second, and both progress step by step in proportion. Both parts express change. Like “as ..., gradually ...”.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + につれて (common: 「時間が経つにつれて」, 「年をとるにつれて」)
examples: As time passed, the sadness faded too.
As my Japanese improved, life in Japan became more fun.
As I've gotten older, I've come to remember the past more often.

senses.label: With nouns of change
senses.meaning: It can follow nouns that already contain the idea of change, such as 「成長」, 「変化」, 「発展」 or 「進歩」.
senses.connection: Noun of change + につれて
examples: As the economy developed, people's lives became richer.
As the children grew, the house started to feel smaller.

notes: The second part must also be a gradual change, not a one-time action or the speaker's intention. ✕「暗くなるにつれて、帰ろう」.
It can't follow nouns with no idea of change. ✕「雨につれて」.
The 「連れて」 in 「子どもを公園に連れて行く」 means “to take (someone) along”. It is not this pattern.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with family as the season changes.
daily.example: As autumn deepens, mornings and evenings have gotten cold, haven't they?

daily.title: Talking about studying
daily.description: Telling a friend what learning a language is like.
daily.example: As I've made progress, I've come to see how interesting Japanese is.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Novels use it to describe a gradual change of mood.
daily.example: As the night wore on, his anxiety grew.

work.title: Analyzing business changes
work.description: Explaining in a meeting how size and costs are related.
work.example: As the business expands, management costs are also increasing.

work.title: A new employee settling in
work.description: A boss comments on a new employee's growth.
work.example: As they've gotten used to the job, they've been making fewer mistakes.

etymology: 「つれる」 is written 「連れる」 and originally means “to take along, accompany”. 「〜につれて」 is “being taken along by ...”, so one change drags another along with it. As a grammar pattern it is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: In the “as ...” meaning they are interchangeable. 「〜にしたがって」 is slightly more formal and also means “according to (rules, instructions)”. 「〜につれて」 only shows proportional change.

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: 「〜に伴って」 is more formal and can describe a one-time accompanying event (法律改正に伴って手続きが変わる). 「〜につれて」 stresses gradual, continuous change.

similar.title: 〜ば〜ほど
similar.explanation: 「〜ば〜ほど」 means “the more ..., the more ...”, stressing a proportional degree, and the second part can be an evaluation. 「〜につれて」 focuses on the process of change over time.

similar.title: 〜一方だ
similar.explanation: 「〜一方だ」 only describes one thing changing steadily in one direction. 「〜につれて」 links two changes together.

meaning: Means “together with ...”, and also “as ...” or “at the same time as ...”. More formal than 「と一緒に」.
connection: Noun + とともに; verb dictionary form, い-adjective, noun + である + とともに

senses.label: Together with ...
senses.meaning: Doing something together with someone or something. The formal version of 「〜と一緒に」, common in speeches, news and writing.
senses.connection: Noun (person, organization, etc.) + とともに
examples: I welcomed the new year with my family.
We will work on community development together with all of you in the area.

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: As the first thing changes, the second changes too. Both parts are changes. Close in meaning to 「〜につれて」, but more formal.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun of change + とともに
examples: As I've gotten older, my memory has weakened.
As the economy developed, environmental problems became serious.

senses.label: At the same time as ...
senses.meaning: Two things happen at the same time, or the same thing has two sides at once. Like “at the same time as ...” or “both ... and ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + とともに; noun / な-adjective + であるとともに
examples: I decided to go back to my hometown upon graduating.
When the exam ended I felt relieved, and at the same time a little lonely.
He is both a doctor and a writer.

notes: This is written language. In everyday speech, “together with ...” is usually 「〜と一緒に」.
It can be written with kanji: 「と共に」.
In the “at the same time” meaning it is close to 「〜と同時に」, but 「と同時に」 stresses the exact same moment more.

daily.title: Writing a New Year's card
daily.description: Formal greetings in a New Year's card or letter.
daily.example: My family and I wish you all good health.

daily.title: Looking back on how you've changed
daily.description: Reflecting on your changes on social media.
daily.example: As I've gotten older, my favorite foods have changed too.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports describe things happening at the same time.
daily.example: As soon as the earthquake struck, power outages occurred in many areas.

work.title: Corporate message
work.description: Expressing growth with customers at a company event or on a website.
work.example: We aim to be a company that grows together with our customers.

work.title: Personnel announcement
work.description: A formal notice that a transfer and promotion happen together.
work.example: Effective April 1, I will be transferred and at the same time appointed section manager.

etymology: 「とも」 is written 「共」 and means “together, jointly”. 「と＋共に」 is “together with ...”, and from “jointly” came the meanings “at the same time” and “as ...”.

similar.title: 〜と同時に
similar.explanation: Both can mean “at the same time”. 「〜と同時に」 stresses that the moments match almost exactly. 「〜とともに」 also means “together” and “as ...”, so it is broader.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: In the “as ...” meaning they are close. 「〜につれて」 stresses gradual proportional change and is more conversational. 「〜とともに」 is more formal and can also describe a one-time simultaneous event.

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: 「〜に伴って」 means “along with ... (something happens)”, but it can't mean “together with a person”. 「〜とともに」 can.

meaning: Two things happen at almost the same moment, or the same thing has two qualities at once. Like “at the same time as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + と同時に; noun / な-adjective + であると同時に

senses.label: At the same moment
senses.meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, the second happens too, with almost no gap in time. Like “the moment ...” or “as soon as ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + と同時に; noun + と同時に (「発売と同時に」, 「到着と同時に」)
examples: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
The new game sold out as soon as it was released.
It started to rain just as I got home.

senses.label: Both at once
senses.meaning: The same thing has two qualities or roles at once, or two feelings arise together. Like “both ... and ...” or “while also ...”.
senses.connection: Noun / な-adjective + であると同時に; verb / adjective plain form + と同時に
examples: He is a teacher and, at the same time, the father of two children.
I'm happy I passed, but at the same time I'm a little anxious.

notes: 「同時に」 on its own is an adverb meaning “simultaneously”, and is not this pattern: 「二つのことを同時にする」.
Unlike 「〜とたん（に）」, 「〜と同時に」 has no sense of surprise, and the second part can be a deliberate action.

daily.title: Leaving work
daily.description: Telling a friend you left work right on time.
daily.example: The moment it hit quitting time, I left the office.

daily.title: Talking about a sellout
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about limited items selling out.
daily.example: Apparently the tickets sold out the moment sales opened.

daily.title: Mixed feelings
daily.description: Telling a friend how you feel at graduation.
daily.example: Graduating makes me happy, but at the same time a bit sad.

work.title: Announcing a product
work.description: A press release explains the launch schedule.
work.example: The new service will become available as soon as the app is released.

work.title: Describing a role
work.description: Introducing an employee who holds two roles.
work.example: He is an engineer and, at the same time, the team leader.

etymology: 「同時」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “the same time”. 「〜と同時に」 is “at the same moment as ...”, and from timing it extended to “having two sides at once”.

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: 「〜とともに」 can also mean “together” and “as ...”, so it is broader. 「〜と同時に」 only means “at the same time”, with a stronger sense of the same moment.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「〜たとたん」 means “the instant ..., (unexpectedly) ...”. The second part is something unexpected and can't be the speaker's deliberate action. 「〜と同時に」 has no surprise, and the second part can be deliberate.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: When meaning “having two sides”, 「〜一方で」 focuses on contrast, while 「〜と同時に」 focuses on both sides existing together.

meaning: A situation continues or is spread over a rough range between two points in time or two places. Like “from ... through ...” or “in the area from ... to ...”.
connection: Noun (time / place) + から + noun (time / place) + にかけて

senses.label: Range of time
senses.meaning: Shows a rough period of time. Unlike 「〜から〜まで」, the start and end are not exact; it stresses “during this stretch”. Common in weather forecasts, seasons and how long events last.
senses.connection: Time noun + から + time noun + にかけて (「今夜から明日にかけて」, 「3月から5月にかけて」)
examples: Heavy rain is expected from tonight through tomorrow morning.
Cherry blossoms bloom from the end of March to early April.
The shop is closed over the New Year holidays.

senses.label: Range of places
senses.meaning: Shows a rough geographical area, the stretch from one place to another. Common when describing weather, disasters or distribution.
senses.connection: Place noun + から + place noun + にかけて (「関東から東北にかけて」)
examples: Heavy rain fell over a wide area from Kyushu to Kanto.
I have pain from my shoulders down my back.

senses.label: Without the start point
senses.meaning: Sometimes 「から」 is left out and only 「〜にかけて」 is used, meaning “(continuing) toward ...”. Common in weather forecasts.
senses.connection: Time noun + にかけて (「夕方にかけて」, 「週末にかけて」)
examples: The rain is expected to get heavier toward the evening.
Temperatures will likely drop toward the weekend.

notes: 「〜から〜まで」 has a clear start and end. 「〜から〜にかけて」 shows a rough range, and the second part is usually a continuing or widespread state.
It can't be used for a specific one-time action: ✕「9時から10時にかけて会議をする」. Say 「9時から10時まで」.
「〜にかけては」 means “when it comes to ... (someone is the best)”. That is a different pattern.

daily.title: Watching the weather forecast
daily.description: Something you often hear on the morning forecast.
daily.example: Rain with thunder is expected from early afternoon into the night.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Discussing with a friend when to travel.
daily.example: June through August is the best season in Hokkaido.

daily.title: Describing symptoms to a doctor
daily.description: Explaining where it hurts.
daily.example: It's been hurting from my neck down to my shoulders.

work.title: Holiday closure notice
work.description: A shop or company announces its holiday schedule.
work.example: We will be closed from December 29 through January 3.

work.title: Disaster news
work.description: News explains the area that was affected.
work.example: Due to the typhoon, heavy damage occurred from western to eastern Japan.

etymology: 「かける」 is written 「掛ける」 and has the sense of “to span, to stretch across”. 「〜から〜にかけて」 originally meant “stretching from ... to ...”, that is, “spanning this range”, so it shows a rough interval.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: 「〜から〜まで」 has a clear start and end and can be used for specific actions (9時から5時まで働く). 「〜から〜にかけて」 is a vague range, mostly for continuing or widespread states.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: 「〜にわたって」 stresses that the whole range is covered, on a large scale (3日間にわたって). 「〜にかけて」 only gives a rough interval.

similar.title: 〜を通して
similar.explanation: 「一年を通して」 means “throughout the whole ... (all the time)”. 「〜から〜にかけて」 only shows a rough interval.

meaning: Something is done or happens with a person, place or thing as its center or main focus. Like “centered on ...” or “mainly ...”.
connection: Noun + を中心に(して) / を中心として / を中心とした + noun

senses.label: Centered on ...
senses.meaning: A place or person is the center in space or in an organization, and things revolve around it.
senses.connection: Noun + を中心に(して) / を中心として
examples: The earth revolves around the sun.
This team is united around Tanaka-san.
Shopping streets spread out around the station.

senses.label: Mainly ...
senses.meaning: A certain range or content is the main focus, but not the only thing. Often used for where something is popular, what an activity covers, or which areas were hit by a disaster.
senses.connection: Noun + を中心に + verb; noun + を中心とした + noun
examples: This anime is popular mainly among young people.
This exam will focus mainly on grammar.
Heavy snow fell in areas centered on the Kanto region.

notes: To modify a noun, use 「〜を中心とした＋noun」 or 「〜を中心とする＋noun」.
The range after 「を中心に」 is not limited to that one item; it means “mainly this, including what's around it”.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Telling a friend what kind of books you read.
daily.example: Lately I've been reading mostly mysteries.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Deciding where to base yourself.
daily.example: I'm planning to base myself in Kyoto and also visit Nara and Osaka.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News explains where something is spreading or where damage occurred.
daily.example: The flu is spreading, mainly among children.

work.title: Explaining your business
work.description: Telling a client about your company's main business.
work.example: Our company operates mainly in Asia.

work.title: Setting the meeting agenda
work.description: Explaining the focus before a meeting.
work.example: In today's meeting, I'd like to focus our discussion on next year's budget.

etymology: 「中心」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “center, core”. 「〜を中心に（する）」 is “making ... the center”, which extended from a spatial center to the main focus of content or scope.

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: 「〜をはじめ」 names one representative example and adds that there are others of the same kind (“starting with ...”). 「〜を中心に」 stresses the core or focus, with other things around it.

similar.title: 〜をもとに
similar.explanation: 「〜をもとに」 means using ... as material or a basis (小説を基に映画を作る). 「〜を中心に」 means making ... the core or focus.

similar.title: 〜のもとで
similar.explanation: 「〜のもとで」 means “under the influence or guidance of ...”. 「〜を中心に」 means “revolving around ...”.

meaning: Names the most representative example and shows there are others of the same kind. Like “starting with ...” or “..., as well as ...”.
connection: Noun + をはじめ(として) / をはじめとする + noun

senses.label: Starting with ...
senses.meaning: First names the main or most typical item, then mentions others of the same kind. The second part often has words of scope like 「など」, 「多くの」, 「さまざまな」 or 「皆」.
senses.connection: Noun + をはじめ(として)、…など / 皆
examples: Starting with the president, all the employees attended the meeting.
Kyoto has many famous temples, starting with Kinkaku-ji.
I'm studying Japanese, as well as Korean and Chinese.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜をはじめとする＋noun」 or 「〜をはじめとした＋noun」 modifies the following noun: “... such as, led by ...”. Mostly written language.
senses.connection: Noun + をはじめとする / をはじめとした + noun
examples: In big cities such as Tokyo, rent is expensive.
Japanese food, with sushi as a prime example, is popular overseas too.

notes: In kanji it is 「始め」, and 「初め」 is also seen, but as a grammar pattern it is usually written in kana: 「はじめ」.
In 「仕事を始める」 or 「勉強を始めた」, it is the verb “to begin”, not this pattern.
The second part can't refer only to the item you named. It must include others of the same kind.

daily.title: Introducing your hometown
daily.description: Telling a foreign friend about famous sights.
daily.example: Nara has many old temples, starting with Todai-ji.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Talking about everyone in the family at a gathering.
daily.example: Everyone in my family is well, including my grandparents.

daily.title: Reading a travel guide
daily.description: Travel guides often use it to introduce local specialties.
daily.example: This region is famous for producing fruit, apples above all.

work.title: Opening remarks
work.description: Thanking attendees at a formal event.
work.example: Today we are honored to welcome Mayor ○○ and many other guests.

work.title: Company profile
work.description: Introducing the company's product line.
work.example: Our company manufactures electronic devices such as smartphones.

etymology: 「はじめ」 is written 「始め」, a noun formed from the stem of the verb 「始める」, meaning “the beginning, the first one”. 「〜をはじめ」 is “taking ... as the first (in a list)”, hence “starting with ...”.

similar.title: 〜を中心に
similar.explanation: 「〜を中心に」 stresses the core or main focus. 「〜をはじめ」 just names a representative first example, with the point being that there are many more of the same kind.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「〜や〜など」 lists examples on an equal footing. 「〜をはじめ」 highlights the first item as the most important or representative, and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 「AばかりでなくBも」 means “not only A but also B”, focusing on widening the scope. 「Aをはじめ」 means “A and many others like it”.

meaning: Putting a feeling, wish or intention into an action or thing. Like “with (love, gratitude) ...” or “full of ...”.
connection: Noun (心・愛・感謝・願い・思い etc.) + を込めて / を込めた + noun

senses.label: Doing with feeling
senses.meaning: Doing something with a certain feeling or intention. It usually follows nouns of feeling like 「心」, 「愛」, 「感謝」, 「願い」, 「思い」 or 「祈り」.
senses.connection: Noun of feeling + を込めて + verb (「心を込めて作る」, 「感謝を込めて贈る」)
examples: I put my heart into making a cake for my mother.
I wrote the letter with feelings of gratitude.
We rang the bell with a wish for peace.

senses.label: Filled with ...
senses.meaning: 「〜を込めた＋noun」 means “(something) filled with ...”. The passive 「〜が込められている」 shows that a work contains a certain feeling.
senses.connection: Noun of feeling + を込めた + noun; noun + が込められている
examples: This is a sweater my grandmother knitted by hand with love.
I threw the ball with all my strength.

notes: 「力を込める」 means “to put strength into, to use force”. This concrete use is also common.
It is usually written 「込めて」, also 「こめて」 in kana. An older spelling is 「籠めて」.

daily.title: Writing a birthday card
daily.description: Writing wishes on a card for a friend.
daily.example: Happy birthday, with all my heart!

daily.title: Giving a present
daily.description: Telling someone what your gift means.
daily.example: As a token of my thanks, I've prepared a small present.

daily.title: Reading song lyrics
daily.description: Common in pop song lyrics.
daily.example: This song is filled with feelings for a friend who passed away.

work.title: Shop promotion
work.description: A restaurant or shop describes its products.
work.example: Our craftspeople make each one with great care.

work.title: Thank-you letter
work.description: A company's letter thanking its customers.
work.example: To thank you for your continued patronage, we are holding a special sale.

etymology: 「こめる」 is written 「込める」 (older 「籠める」) and originally means “to load, to pack in”, as in 「弾を込める」 (load a bullet). From “putting something in” it came to mean “putting feelings into” something.

similar.title: 〜を持って
similar.explanation: 「自信を持って」 and 「勇気を持って」 mean “with (a certain attitude or state of mind)”. 「〜を込めて」 means pouring feelings into an action or work, stressing deep investment.

similar.title: 〜を通して
similar.explanation: 「〜を通して」 means conveying something through a means or medium. 「〜を込めて」 means putting your feelings into the action itself.

meaning: Achieving something by means of a person or thing; also “throughout” a period or range. Like “through ...” or “throughout ...”.
connection: Noun + を通して / を通じて (written: を通し・を通じ)

senses.label: Through (a means)
senses.meaning: Getting a result by means of an experience, activity or medium. Like “through ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (経験・活動・テレビ・インターネット etc.) + を通して / を通じて
examples: I learned many things through studying abroad.
Through the internet, you can interact with people all over the world.
I made lots of friends through volunteer work.

senses.label: Through a person
senses.meaning: Communicating or making contact through an intermediary. Like “via ...”. More indirect and formal than contacting someone directly.
senses.connection: Person / organization noun + を通して / を通じて + 伝える / 申し込む etc.
examples: Through a senior colleague, I was able to meet the president.
We will contact you with the details through my secretary.

senses.label: Throughout
senses.meaning: After a noun of time or range, it means “all through the whole ...”. Like “all year round” or “throughout ...”.
senses.connection: Time / range noun (一年・年間・生涯・全国 etc.) + を通して / を通じて
examples: This region is warm all year round.
Tourists visit this island throughout the year.

notes: 「を通して」 and 「を通じて」 mean basically the same. 「を通じて」 is slightly more formal, while 「を通して」 stresses deliberately using a means.
The 「通って」 in 「公園を通って帰る」 means “to pass through” physically. It is not this pattern.
In writing, 「を通し、」 and 「を通じ、」 are used.

daily.title: Talking about learning Japanese
daily.description: Telling a friend how you learned Japanese.
daily.example: I learned Japanese through anime.

daily.title: Recommending a destination
daily.description: Recommending a place that's good to visit any time of year.
daily.example: You can enjoy a trip to Okinawa all year round.

daily.title: Being introduced
daily.description: Meeting someone through a friend.
daily.example: I met my current girlfriend through a friend.

work.title: Formal communication
work.description: Contacting a company through the person in charge.
work.example: From now on, please contact us through Yamada, who is in charge.

work.title: Corporate social contribution
work.description: A company explains the meaning of its activities.
work.example: Our company aims to contribute to society through our business.

etymology: 「通す」 means “to let through, to pass through”, and 「通じる」 means “to lead to, to connect”. Both come from the idea of “going through from one end to the other”, which extended to “via a medium” and “all the way through a period”.

similar.title: 〜を通じて・〜を通して (N2)
similar.explanation: When the same pattern appears again at N2, the focus is on more formal uses such as 「生涯を通じて」 and 「全国を通じて」. The meaning is the same.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「〜によって」 shows a means, method or cause, and is more objective, as in 「機械によって作る」. 「〜を通して」 stresses going through an experience, medium or intermediary, with a sense of process.

similar.title: 〜から〜にかけて
similar.explanation: 「〜から〜にかけて」 shows a rough interval. 「一年を通して」 means it stays the same throughout the whole period.
